note: Authored blind: written by reading the source PDFs directly, before running the queries, so no question was tuned to what retrieval happens to return. Gold labels are (source_file, page) rather than chunk ids so they survive a re-chunk. `expected` lists the acceptable LOCATIONS of one intended answer (a concept slide and its pseudocode slide are the same answer), not several distinct answers. Image-only and TOC pages are excluded as unfair targets: module05.pdf pages 2/3/5/33/35/38 are Outline slides, and pages 15/20/24/25/28/29 chunk down to bare diagram captions ('Height decrease', 'get-predecessors(52)') with no answerable text.
revisions: 2026-07-26 (m*/a*): 12 questions over module05 + a3-a5, a 52-chunk corpus. 2026-07-26 (n*): 18 added when the corpus grew to 181 chunks over 10 documents (module01/03/05, tut01sol, a0-a5). The original 12 are unchanged and their gold pages still resolve. The n* set deliberately targets the confusability the bigger corpus introduced: three documents now cover asymptotic notation (module01 defines it, tut01sol proves it, a1 asks about it) and two cover sorting.

queries.query: Why can't we use binary search on an ordered linked list?
queries.note: Slide 'Towards skip lists': in an ordered list we cannot 'skip to the middle', so search is Theta(n).

queries.query: What two references does each node of a skip list store?
queries.note: 'Each node p has references p.after and p.below'.

queries.query: How is the height of a key's tower chosen when inserting into a skip list?
queries.note: p21 states it in prose (repeatedly toss a coin until tails); p30 is the same rule as pseudocode (`for (i <- 0; random(2) = 1; i++)`). Either is a correct hit.

queries.query: What is the expected space usage and expected run-time of skip list operations?
queries.note: Analysis slide and summary slide: O(n) expected space, O(log n) expected time for all operations. Known hazard: a4.pdf p1 asks the student to DERIVE this bound. The lecture states the result, so a4 p1 is a miss, not a hit.

queries.query: What does the move-to-front heuristic do after a successful search?
queries.note: 'Upon a successful search, move the accessed item to the front of the list'.

queries.query: What is the transpose heuristic, and how does it differ from move-to-front?
queries.note: 'swap the accessed item with the item immediately preceding it' — changes are more gradual than MTF.

queries.query: Which ordering of a list minimizes the average access cost when the access frequencies are known?
queries.note: p36 defines average access cost; p37 states the claim: sort by non-increasing access-frequency.

queries.query: What is the worst-case runtime of interpolation search on an array with entries A[i] = alpha * i?
queries.note: Assignment 4 Question 3(a), Interpolation search.

queries.query: Trace the construction of the Huffman trie for the string mississauga.
queries.note: Assignment 5 Question 4(a). 'mississauga' is a strong lexical anchor — should be easy.

queries.query: When is Assignment 4 due and what is its late policy?
queries.note: Deliberate hard case. a3.pdf p1 and a5.pdf p1 carry near-identical due-date boilerplate differing only in the dates, which dense retrieval is expected to confuse. A fair target for Phase 4 to fix.

queries.query: Describe an algorithm that merges two AVL trees whose heights are given.
queries.note: Assignment 3 Question 3, 'Merging AVL Trees', Join(TA, TB, hA, hB).

queries.query: How is the spread of a point set defined, and what does it imply about quadtree height?
queries.note: Assignment 5 Question 2(a)/(b): quadtree of height exactly 6, and the spread of a point set.

queries.query: What does the RAM model assume about the cost of accessing memory cells?
queries.note: Slide 'Random access machine (RAM) model': random access, equally fast to all cells, unbounded cell size.

queries.query: What is the definition of Theta-notation in terms of the constants c1, c2 and n0?
queries.note: Slide 'Asymptotic tight bound'. HARD (m5/m6 pattern): a1.pdf p1 poses Theta problems and tut01sol.pdf proves Theta statements, so the lecture DEFINITION competes with an assignment question and a tutorial proof on the same notation.

queries.query: What is the main difference between o-notation and O-notation?
queries.note: 'Main difference between o and O is the quantifier for c'. HARD (near-duplicate): module01 p26/p29 also discuss o-notation, and o-notation appears again in tut01sol.pdf and a1.pdf.

queries.query: What is the limit rule for comparing the growth rates of two functions?
queries.note: Slide 'The limit rule': the value of lim f(x)/g(x) determines which order relation holds.

queries.query: What recurrence does merge-sort satisfy and what does it resolve to?
queries.note: p49 sets up the exact recurrence, p50 simplifies it, p51 summarises, p52 tabulates T(n) <= 2T(n/2) + O(n) -> O(n log n). Any is a correct location for the one answer.

queries.query: What are the four steps for giving an algorithm that solves a problem?
queries.note: 'To give an algorithm that solves a problem, we usually do four steps', illustrated on merge-sort.

queries.query: What is the difference between average-case run-time and expected run-time?
queries.note: Slide 'Summary: Average-case run-time vs. expected run-time' — the answer is 'No!' plus the distinction. HARD (m5/m6 pattern): a2.pdf poses average-case counting problems on the same idea.

queries.query: What is the expected run-time of randomized quick-select?
queries.note: Theta(n). p29/p30 derive the recurrence, p31 states it. HARD (confusable pair): near-identical phrasing to n9, six slides apart, different answer.

queries.query: What is the expected run-time of randomized quick-sort?
queries.note: Theta(n log n). HARD (confusable pair): the deliberate twin of n8. If dense retrieval crosses these two, hybrid retrieval should be what separates them.

queries.query: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be comparison-based?
queries.note: 'Data is accessed only by comparing two elements (a key-comparison)', on the sorting lower-bound slide.

queries.query: In what order does LSD-radix-sort process the digits?
queries.note: 'for d <- least significant to most significant digit'. Competes with MSD-radix-sort on p68.

queries.query: Prove that log(n!) is in Theta(n log n).
queries.note: Tutorial 01 question 3, 'Factorials'. Statement on p2, proof continues on p3. HARD (near-duplicate): module01 covers Theta and logarithm facts; this is the tutorial's worked proof.

queries.query: For the function that equals n squared when n is even and n when n is odd, is it in O(n squared)?
queries.note: Tutorial 01 question 4, 'Parity'. Question on p3, answers on p4. HARD (near-duplicate): O/Omega/Theta/o reasoning also appears in module01 and a1.

queries.query: Is heapsort a stable sorting algorithm?
queries.note: Assignment 2 Question 4. HARD (m5/m6 pattern, inverted): the ASSIGNMENT is the right answer here, competing against module03's sorting slides.

queries.query: What is an inversion in an array, and what are the maximum and minimum numbers of inversions?
queries.note: Assignment 2 Question 6: 'a pair of indices (i, j) such that i < j and A[i] > A[j]'.

queries.query: Leo's induction proof ends with a different constant than the induction hypothesis — why is that wrong?
queries.note: Assignment 1 Question 3, the TA-Leo scenario. HARD (exact-token): 'Leo' is a rare literal token that appears nowhere else in the corpus, so this probes whether dense retrieval can use a distinctive name.

queries.query: How do I include an image of handwritten work in a LaTeX assignment?
queries.note: Assignment 0 section 'Images'. Administrative rather than technical content — a KB holds both.

queries.query: When is the first Academic Integrity Declaration due and which assignments does it cover?
queries.note: Assignment 0: the first agreement covers A0, A1, A2 and PQ1. HARD (exact-token): 'Academic Integrity Declaration' and the identifier 'PQ1' are literal strings, the kind of query dense embeddings typically handle worse than BM25.
